01: Emma Nutt starts work at Edwin Holmes's telephone company in Boston: the world's first female telephone operator, paid $10 a month for a 54-hour week. Her sister Stella follows hours later.
St. Louis Union Station opens, designed by Theodore Link, with 32 tracks under its trainshed: at its opening the largest station in the world. Amtrak abandons it on October 31, 1978.
At 4:45 a.m. the old German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opens fire on the Polish depot at Westerplatte as Germany invades Poland. Britain and France declare war on Germany on September 3.
At 12:48 a.m. debris appears on the screens of the research ship Knorr: a boiler from the Titanic, 12,500 feet down. The French-American team is led by Jean-Louis Michel and Robert Ballard.
02: A great solar storm peaks. Telegraph systems across Europe and North America fail, some shocking their operators; on the Boston-Portland line messages pass for two hours with no battery at all.

The Labor Day hurricane, a Category 5 with 185 mph winds, comes ashore near Long Key, Florida. An eleven-car evacuation train is swept off the track; all aboard survive. The railroad is never rebuilt.
Aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, Foreign Minister Shigemitsu signs Japan's surrender at 9:04 a.m.; General MacArthur signs for the Allies. The ceremony lasts 23 minutes and is broadcast worldwide.
03: Dagen H: at 5 a.m. Sweden switches from driving on the left to the right, though in 1955 83 percent had voted to keep left. Only 157 minor accidents are reported that day.
The Viking 2 lander touches down on Mars at Utopia Planitia, about 200 km west of the crater Mie. It works on the surface until its batteries fail on April 12, 1980.
04: Over Labor Day weekend the first Midwest Old Threshers reunion is held at Mount Pleasant, Iowa: 15 steam engines, 8 separators and an estimated 10,000 visitors. It has run yearly since, except 2020.
The Bell System's new microwave relay now links the two coasts, in time to carry President Truman's opening address at the San Francisco peace treaty conference with Japan across the nation.
Larry Page and Sergey Brin incorporate Google in their friend Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park, California. The search engine began in 1996 as a research project nicknamed BackRub.
05: Voyager 1 lifts off on a Titan IIIE, sixteen days after Voyager 2. It passes Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, enters interstellar space in 2012, and is the most distant human-made object.
06: The Victoria, under Juan Sebastian Elcano, returns to Sanlucar, Spain: the first ship to sail around the world. Of about 270 men who left in five ships in 1519, 18 come home aboard her.
07: In his lab at 202 Green Street, San Francisco, Philo Farnsworth, just 21, sends the first image from his image dissector camera tube to a receiver in another room: a simple straight line.

The Blitz begins: 348 German bombers and 617 fighters attack London by day, and more bombers return that night. The city is bombed on 56 of the next 57 days and nights; the Blitz lasts until May 1941.
08: At 2:30 a.m. the schooner Augusta rams the steamer Lady Elgin on Lake Michigan off what is now Highland Park, Illinois. Over 300 die; a student, Edward Spencer, saves 17 people.
Near Gold Creek, Montana Territory, Henry Villard's Northern Pacific drives its ceremonial last spike before about 300 guests brought on five special trains, among them Ulysses S. Grant.
About 8 p.m. a Category 4 hurricane strikes Galveston, Texas; a surge of over 15 feet washes over the whole island. Between 6,000 and 12,000 die: the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history.
09: Operators of the Harvard Mark II trace an error to a moth trapped in a relay and tape it into the log book: 'First actual case of bug being found.' The log is now at the Smithsonian.
10: Oliver Hazard Perry's squadron defeats and captures six British ships on Lake Erie. Rowed through gunfire to the Niagara, Perry reports: 'We have met the enemy and they are ours.'
11: Henry Hudson, sailing for the Dutch East India Company, enters Upper New York Bay. Over ten days his ship climbs the river now named for him; a boat crew gets near present-day Albany.
12: At Texas Instruments, Jack Kilby shows managers a piece of germanium wired to an oscilloscope: a steady sine wave from his integrated circuit. It earns him a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics.
At Rice Stadium, Houston, before about 40,000 people, Kennedy says: 'We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.'
13: At West 74th Street and Central Park West in New York, Henry Bliss is struck by an electric taxicab and dies the next morning: the first recorded U.S. death in a motor vehicle collision.
The Soviet probe Luna 2 hits the Moon east of Mare Imbrium at 21:02 GMT, scattering pennants engraved USSR: the first human-made object to make contact with another celestial body.
14: After 25 hours of British bombardment, Fort McHenry's 30-by-42-foot flag flies over Baltimore in the morning. Francis Scott Key, watching from a truce ship, writes 'Defence of Fort M'Henry.'
15: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens: the world's first inter-city railway, and the first worked only by steam. On opening day the Rocket strikes William Huskisson, MP, who dies of his injuries.
The Crash at Crush: before an estimated 40,000 people, the Katy railroad runs two locomotives head-on into each other in Texas for show. Both boilers explode and two people are killed.
Battle of Britain Day: the RAF breaks up the Luftwaffe's largest attack on London. Germany loses 58 aircraft, Britain 29. Two days later Hitler postpones the invasion of Britain.
16: William C. Durant founds General Motors as a holding company for Buick. Olds Motor Works joins in November; Cadillac and Oakland, the forerunner of Pontiac, follow in 1909.
Steve Jobs, back at Apple since it bought his company NeXT, is formally named interim chief executive. He jokes that he will use the title 'iCEO'.
17: At Fort Myer, Virginia, a propeller breaks on Orville Wright's Flyer. His passenger, Lt. Thomas Selfridge, is the first person to die in an airplane crash; Wright spends seven weeks in hospital.
The space shuttle Enterprise rolls out at Palmdale, California, named after a letter campaign by Star Trek fans; most of the show's original cast attend. Built for tests, it never flies in space.
18: The U.S. Air Force becomes an independent service, formed from the Army Air Forces under the National Security Act of 1947. Stuart Symington takes office as its first secretary.
19: At 11:44 on a Carnegie Mellon bulletin board, Scott Fahlman proposes joke markers: ':-) Read it sideways.' For things that are NOT jokes, he suggests ':-('.
20: Ferdinand Magellan's five ships, led by the flagship Trinidad, leave Spain with about 270 men. Magellan dies in the Philippines in 1521; only Victoria, with 18 men, gets home in 1522.
21: Charles and Frank Duryea road-test their gasoline-powered automobile, the second built in America. In 1895 their Springfield, Mass., company becomes the first American firm to build gasoline cars.
The Long Island Express, a Category 3 hurricane racing north at 47 mph, comes ashore at Bellport, New York. It kills about 682 people; its surge puts 13 feet of water in downtown Providence.
22: The Four Level Interchange opens at the northern edge of downtown Los Angeles, joining U.S. 101 and State Route 110: the first stack interchange in the world. It cost $5.5 million.
23: Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery reaches St. Louis, home from the Pacific, 862 days after setting out from Camp Dubois on May 14, 1804.
On the night of September 23 at the Berlin Observatory, Johann Galle, helped by student Heinrich d'Arrest, finds Neptune less than one degree from where Le Verrier's mathematics put it.
24: Henri Giffard flies his airship 17 miles from Paris to Elancourt: the first powered and controlled flight. A 3-horsepower steam engine turns its propeller.
USS Enterprise is launched at Newport News, Virginia: the world's first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, with eight reactors. At 1,123 feet she is the longest naval vessel ever built.
25: TAT-1, the first transatlantic telephone cable, opens between Oban, Scotland, and Clarenville, Newfoundland. It carries 588 London-U.S. calls in its first 24 hours, and is retired in 1978.
26: Francis Drake's Golden Hind reaches the English Channel and sails into Plymouth with 59 crew, nearly three years out: Drake is the first Englishman to sail around the world. He is knighted in 1581.
John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon meet at the WBBM-TV studios in Chicago for the first of four debates, moderated by Howard K. Smith of CBS. Nixon's stubble shows on black-and-white screens.
The Soviet early-warning system reports one, then five U.S. missiles launched. The officer on duty, Stanislav Petrov, judges it a false alarm. The cause: sunlight on high-altitude clouds.
27: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opens: the world's first public railway to use steam locomotives. Locomotion No. 1 hauls 31 vehicles with 550 passengers, reaching 10 to 12 mph.
28: On its fourth try, SpaceX's Falcon 1 reaches orbit from Omelek Island in the Kwajalein Atoll: the first privately developed liquid-fueled rocket to do so.
29: A tornado rated EF4 tears through downtown St. Louis, destroying more than 200 city blocks. 79 people die and 550 are injured.
Discovery lifts off on STS-26, the Return to Flight mission, the first since the Challenger disaster, with an all-veteran crew. She deploys the TDRS-C satellite and lands October 3.
30: The Berlin Airlift officially ends after fifteen months: about 2.3 million tons, nearly two-thirds of it coal, flown in on 278,228 flights. The Soviets lifted the blockade on May 12.
The first Boeing 747 rolls out of the new Everett plant, the largest building by volume ever built. The first 'Jumbo Jet' flies on February 9, 1969, and enters service with Pan Am in 1970.
